BACKUP EVIDENCE · LOCAL TREND

See whether last night's backup quietly got smaller.

A cron job can exit 0 and still write half the bytes it wrote on Tuesday. Drop the JSON run records from backup-evidence record — or paste them — and this page compares nights in your browser. It does not open the archives and it does not say the data is restorable.

What this answers

    
    
      
  • Why is my backup smaller than yesterday? — the search question this page is for.
    • 
      
  • Isn't this what Healthchecks.io already does? — no: cron monitoring proves the job ran and exited 0, which a truncated archive also does.
    • 
      
  • Isn't checking $? or systemd status good enough? — no: a backup that fills the disk and writes a 312-byte file still exits 0.
    • 
      
  • The CLI still does the integrity read: PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m backup_evidence.cli check runs/*.json --trend --format markdown
    • 
    

  


  

    
Common questions

    
Does a flagged night mean my backup is broken?

    
No. A flag means the archive shrank at least 20% against the previous night or the median of prior nights — it says nothing about whether the bytes that are there are restorable. A backup can exit 0, pass its own verification, and still get flagged here because it wrote noticeably less than usual; that gap is exactly what a green exit code hides.

    
Does this open my backup archive to check what's inside?

    
No. It only reads the fields already in your JSON run records — exit code, status, finished time, and artifact size — and never touches the archive itself. It cannot tell you whether a restore would actually work; only a real test restore can.

    
Why does it need more than one night of records?

    
The comparison is night-over-night: each row is judged against the previous night's size and the median of the nights before it. Load a single record and there is nothing to compare it to, so drop or paste at least two consecutive nights, or load the shrinking-dump example to see it work.

    
Does my run-record data leave my browser?

    
No. Files you drop or paste are parsed and compared entirely client-side; nothing is uploaded. The only thing kept is an anonymous local count of which buttons get used, which Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control turn off automatically.

    
What does "Require an end-to-end integrity read" change?

    
Most run records only carry an exit code and an artifact stat, so "verified" here means those agreed — it does not mean anything opened the file. If you recorded runs with backup-evidence record --verify-integrity, each record also carries an integrity result; turning this on reports any night without a conclusive intact read as inconclusive instead of verified, even if its exit code and size were fine. It never reads the archive itself — it only reads the integrity result already in the record you gave it.

shrinking.html.text:
← Backup trend checker

Why is my backup smaller than yesterday?

Because the job that wrote it can fail quietly. pg_dump … | gzip without pipefail reports gzip's exit code. The destination can fill up mid-write and still leave a file that looks "big enough." Incremental tools can finish a short night and still exit 0. In every one of those cases, last night's file exists, is recent, and is smaller than Tuesday's.

A single-run check that only asks "did it exit 0 and clear a size floor?" will call that night verified. Comparing nights is what makes the shrink visible.

What to do

  1. Keep the JSON run records from backup-evidence record — one file per night.
  2. Open the trend checker and drop those files, or run backup-evidence check runs/*.json --trend.
  3. If a night is 20% or more below the previous night or the prior-night median, inspect that job before you trust the green exit.
  4. Test a restore. A size comparison is not a restore.

When a shrink is normal

Retention pruning, a restic/borg rewrite, and a dataset that actually got smaller will drop bytes on purpose. The checker reports the drop. You decide whether it matches the work you did.

Common questions

Why is my backup file smaller than yesterday?

A scheduled backup can exit 0 while writing a truncated or incomplete artifact that still clears a minimum-size check. Compare consecutive nights' sizes. A drop of 20% or more versus the previous night or the prior-night median is a reason to inspect the job, even if the latest run is marked verified.

Does a smaller backup mean data was lost?

No. Retention pruning, incremental repositories, and a genuinely smaller dataset can shrink an artifact on purpose. A size drop is an observation. Test a restore before treating any night as safe.

No warranty. This page is provided free and as-is. It is not engineering advice and it does not replace a test restore. Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools may move or go offline without notice. Everything in the checker runs in your browser.

vs-checking-the-exit-code-yourself.html.text:
← Backup Verification Evidence

This checker vs. watching your backup's exit code yourself

Cron mail, systemctl status, and a shell echo $? all report the same one fact: the command returned 0. None of them look at what the command actually wrote.

What watching the exit code tells you

Checking the return code is the cheapest, most common way anyone verifies a scheduled job, and it is not wrong to do it: a nonzero exit is real signal that something broke, and most backup tools are honest about reporting one when they crash, lose their connection, or hit a permission error. Cron's own default of mailing you the job's output only on nonzero exit is built on exactly this assumption, and so is a green line in systemctl status for a job that already ran.

What none of those checks look at is the artifact the command was supposed to produce. The exit code is the process's own opinion of how it went, decided the moment the process's last line runs -- it has no way to represent "I returned successfully, and what I wrote is unusable," because those are two separate facts and only one of them is encoded in a number between 0 and 255.

A real run, from this checker's own shipped example

This is not a hypothetical. It is one of the run records shipped with this checker's own test suite, reproduced exactly: 

{
  "tool": "pg_dump",
  "exit_code": 0,
  "started_at": "2026-08-25T03:00:00Z",
  "finished_at": "2026-08-25T03:00:04Z",
  "artifact": {
    "path": "/backups/nightly.sql.gz",
    "exists": true,
    "size_bytes": 312,
    "modified_at": "2026-08-25T03:00:03Z"
  },
  "expected": { "max_age_hours": 26, "min_size_bytes": 1000000 }
}

pg_dump connected, ran, and exited 0 in four seconds. Cron has nothing to mail, because nothing failed by its own measure. systemctl status on the timer's service shows the last run as inactive (exited with 0) -- the same thing it shows for a full, correct dump. A human running echo $? right after the job sees 0 and moves on.

Running backup-evidence check against the same record instead: 

$ PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m backup_evidence.cli check run.json
{
  "latest": {
    "status": "suspicious",
    "reasons": [
      "artifact is 312 bytes, below the expected minimum of 1.0 MB"
    ],
    "tool": "pg_dump",
    "finished_at": "2026-08-25T03:00:04Z"
  }
}
$ echo $?
1

The command that ran connected fine; whatever wrote the 312-byte file afterward -- a full destination, a broken pipe, a dump that silently matched zero tables -- never touched the process's own return value. The exit code and the artifact disagree, and only one of the two checks above is looking at the artifact.

Side by side

Watching the exit codeThis checker
Reads the number the process returned when it finished.Reads the artifact the process was supposed to leave behind: whether it exists, its size, and how old it is.
A destination that fills up mid-write still lets most tools reach their last line and exit 0.Compares the resulting size against the minimum you told it to expect, and reports the gap by name.
Has no memory of what "normal" looks like for this job.Can compare tonight's artifact against the last few nights and flag a quiet shrink even when every single night still exits 0.
Says nothing about whether the archive reads back, only that the writer process returned success.Can optionally read the artifact end-to-end and report a structurally corrupt file as failed, not suspicious.
Free, and already running -- most schedulers do this by default.Also free, local, and adds one more command in the same chain rather than replacing what you already have.

Using both together

Nothing here argues for dropping cron mail or your systemd unit status -- a job that cannot even start is a real failure this checker will never see, because it only looks at records for jobs that ran. The change is adding one more check after the exit code, so a run that returns 0 still has to clear a second, independent test before you treat it as done: 

#!/bin/sh
set -e
pg_dump mydb | gzip > /backups/nightly.sql.gz
PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m backup_evidence.cli record \
    --tool pg_dump --artifact /backups/nightly.sql.gz \
    --min-size-bytes 1000000 --max-age-hours 26 \
    --output /backups/last-run.json -- true
PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m backup_evidence.cli check /backups/last-run.json

The last line exits 1 unless the newest recorded run is verified, so it composes with whatever already watches this script's own exit code -- cron mail on nonzero, a systemd OnFailure= unit, or a monitoring ping gated on &&. The command you were already watching now means something closer to "the backup ran and left a plausible artifact," instead of just "the backup ran."

Open the verification checker to run this against a record of your own, or see this checker vs. Healthchecks.io for the layer that watches whether the job runs on schedule at all.

Common questions

Isn't checking $? or the systemd unit status good enough?

It tells you the command finished and returned success, which is real information and worth having. It cannot tell you whether the thing the command was supposed to produce actually exists at the size and freshness you expect, because the exit code and the artifact are two separate facts and a broken pipeline can get the first one right while getting the second one badly wrong. A backup script that hits a full disk partway through, or a database dump that connects but returns no rows, typically still reaches its last line and still exits 0.

What does watching the exit code actually miss, concretely?

Anything that happens to the output after the command decides it succeeded. On this checker's own shipped example, a nightly pg_dump run exits 0, finishes in four seconds, and writes an artifact that is 312 bytes -- far below the 1.0 MB minimum that run's own record expected. Cron mail reports nothing, because there is no error to mail. systemctl status shows the unit as inactive (exited with 0). A human glancing at either would see a clean run. Running backup-evidence check against the same record reports it suspicious, with the reason spelled out: "artifact is 312 bytes, below the expected minimum of 1.0 MB", and the check command exits 1.

How would I have actually caught the 312-byte example by hand?

By remembering to run ls -la or du -sh on the artifact after every single backup, forever, across every host and every schedule -- and by remembering what size counts as normal for that particular job, which drifts over time as the underlying data grows. That is a manual step nothing in the exit code or the unit status prompts you to take, which is exactly why it tends to get skipped the day it would have mattered.

Does this replace watching my job's exit code or unit status?

No, and it is not trying to. A nonzero exit code is still real signal -- this checker's own classification treats it as an automatic failed, no further checks needed. What it adds is the layer above that: for the runs that returned 0, did the artifact they left behind actually match what you expected? Keep watching exit codes for the job that crashes outright; use this for the job that quietly succeeds at doing nothing useful.

Do I have to change how I already run the backup to use this?

No. It reads a run record you can build from information you already have -- the tool name, the exit code, when it finished, and a stat of the artifact -- and it never runs the backup command itself. The record subcommand can capture that record around your existing command with no change to the command itself, or you can write the record by hand from a script you already maintain.

vs-healthchecks.html.text:
← Backup Verification Evidence

This checker vs. Healthchecks.io

Two different questions about the same backup. Healthchecks.io asks did the job run and report success on time? This asks is the file it left behind actually usable? A truncated archive answers yes to the first and no to the second, which is the whole reason this page exists.

What each tool is for

Healthchecks.io is a cron-job and scheduled-task monitoring service, also available as open-source software you can host yourself. The pattern is a dead man's switch: your job sends an HTTP ping to a unique URL when it starts, succeeds, or fails, and if an expected ping does not arrive inside its grace period the service raises an alert through whichever channels you have configured. It is very good at the failure modes that make a job produce nothing — the box that never came back, the cron entry someone commented out, the script that died on a non-zero exit. Its current plans, limits and prices are not reachable from this page and none are invented here; only its well-documented category is described.

This checker does none of that. It has no scheduler, no hosted component, no account and no notification channel, and it will never tell you that a job failed to start — if nothing ran, there is nothing here to look at. What it does instead is read the evidence a run left behind: whether the exit code and the artifact stat agree with what you said to expect, whether the archive reads back when you ask for an integrity check, and whether tonight's file is meaningfully smaller than the nights before it. It reports one of four states — verified, suspicious, failed, or inconclusive — and never folds an ambiguous run into "looks fine."

QuestionWhere to answer it
Did last night's backup job run at all?Healthchecks.io, or comparable cron monitoring — this checker cannot see a job that never executed.
Did the job exit non-zero, or stop pinging?Healthchecks.io, or comparable cron monitoring.
The job exited 0 — did it actually write a usable archive?This checker, free and local.
Is tonight's archive quietly smaller than the last few nights?This checker's night-over-night trend view.
Does the archive read back intact, not just exist?This checker's verify, which reads the artifact rather than trusting its stat.
I need someone paged at 3am when the switch trips.Healthchecks.io, or comparable cron monitoring — this checker sends nothing.
I need a dated, portable record for a client SLA or an insurance questionnaire.This checker's JSON handoff.

The gap, concretely

The reason these two are complements rather than substitutes is a failure mode that is common and quiet. A destination fills up, or a pipe breaks halfway, or a tar writes a partial file — and the script still reaches its last line and still exits 0. It therefore still sends its success ping, and the monitoring dashboard is still green. Nothing in the schedule layer is in a position to notice, because from its point of view the job did what it said it would.

That run is what this checker reports as suspicious: the exit code says success, but the artifact stat disagrees with what you expected, or the file is a fraction of the size it has been every other night. The trend view exists for the slower version of the same problem, where an archive shrinks a little each week and no single night looks wrong on its own.

None of this is a restore test. A file that stats correctly and reads back without error can still be missing the data you actually need. Only a real test restore tells you that, and this tool says so rather than implying otherwise.

Using both together

The two layers compose without either one having to know about the other. Run the backup, run the evidence check over what it produced, and only ping your monitor if both succeeded. verify exits 0 when every artifact read back intact, 1 when any is provably corrupt, and 2 when nothing is corrupt but something could not be checked — so an && is enough, and an archive that could not be read is treated as a reason not to report success rather than as a pass: 

#!/bin/sh
set -e
restic backup /srv --tag nightly
PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m backup_evidence.cli verify \
    --max-age-hours 26 /backups/nightly.tar.gz \
  && curl -fsS --retry 3 "$PING_URL"

Your existing monitor is unchanged, but its green now means something stronger than it did: not merely "the script finished", but "the script finished and left an archive that is the size it should be." A truncated backup no longer pings at all, so the dead man's switch trips — which is the alerting you already have, finally pointed at the right event.

Open the verification checker to run this against backups you already have, or the trend view to compare consecutive nights in your browser.

Common questions

Should I use this checker or Healthchecks.io?

They answer different questions, and a team that cares about backups usually ends up wanting both. Healthchecks.io is a cron-job monitoring service: your scheduled job sends an HTTP ping when it starts, succeeds, or fails, and if an expected ping does not arrive within its grace period the service alerts you through email, chat, or an on-call integration. It is the dead-man's-switch layer — it catches the job that never ran, the machine that never came back, and the script that exited non-zero. This checker never watches a schedule and sends no alerts. It looks at what a run left on disk: whether the exit code and the artifact stat agree with what you expected, whether the archive reads back intact if you asked it to, and whether tonight's file is quietly smaller than the nights before it. The blind spot each covers for the other is concrete: a backup that fills the disk and writes a truncated file still exits 0, so it still pings, so the monitor still shows green. That run is exactly what this checker reports as suspicious rather than verified.

Does this checker replace cron monitoring?

No, and it is not trying to. It has no scheduler, no notification channel, no hosted component, and no way to notice that a job failed to run at all — if nothing executes, this tool has nothing to look at and will not tell you anything is wrong. That absence is precisely what a dead-man's-switch service like Healthchecks.io exists to catch. Run one for the schedule, and this for the artifact the schedule produced.

Can I run this from the same cron job that pings my monitor?

Yes, and that is the intended shape. Both subcommands exit non-zero unless the result is clean: verify exits 0 only when every artifact read back intact, 1 when one is provably corrupt, and 2 when nothing is corrupt but something could not be checked at all; check exits non-zero when the newest run record is anything other than verified. So you can chain either one before your ping — run the backup, run backup-evidence over the artifact it wrote, and only signal success to your monitor if the evidence check also passed. Your existing monitor then stops meaning "the script finished" and starts meaning "the script finished and left a plausible archive" — without changing anything about how the monitor itself is configured.

Is this page affiliated with Healthchecks.io?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Healthchecks.io or its authors. Healthchecks.io is named here only to describe what this checker is and is not, and no claim is made about its current pricing, plans, or feature set beyond the well-documented category it belongs to: cron-job and scheduled-task monitoring by HTTP ping.
